Issued at 442 AM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

A deep longwave trough axis lies from the Pacific Northwest to 
the coastal waters off southern California early this morning. 
Aside from the remnants of Isaias, the Gulf Coast and eastern 
CONUS are under upper level ridging. This places southwest flow 
aloft over the Northern Plains. A surface cold front has cleared
all but the southeast corner of the state and is trailed by a 
low level baroclinic zone. Numerous shortwaves are forecast to 
eject from the base of the western trough today through Monday. 
The associated DCVA paired with broad isentropic ascent keeps 
precipitation chances in the forecast through Monday afternoon, 
diminishing Monday evening and overnight as the deep western 
trough cuts off from the northern stream. The highest chances 
for precipitation (90 to 100 percent) remain confined to west 
central and northern North Dakota, though the rest of our 
forecast area is still likely to see periodic light rain showers
at times (60 to 80 percent chance). The time period with both 
the highest precipitation chances and QPF is tonight into Monday
morning with a more potent mid level shortwave. Mesoscale 
forcing and instability do not appear that impressive, but the 
potential for a long duration of steady precipitation could 
produce QPF as high as one half to one inch, with the HREF 
probability-matched mean showing this potential along and 
northwest of a line from Beach to Bottineau. This lines up with 
the NBM showing high chances for exceeding half an inch and low 
to medium chances for exceeding one inch over this same area.

Very little diurnal heating is expected this afternoon under 
thick cloud cover and north-northeast surface flow reinforcing 
the cooler air mass. Forecast highs today range from the lower 
40s northwest to upper 50s in the southern James River Valley. 
Forecast lows tonight range from near freezing in the northwest 
to the lower and mid 40s southeast. The colder temperatures in 
the northwest could allow rain to mix with or change over to 
snow late tonight into Monday morning, and there is now a 
potential outcome of precipitation remaining snow through Monday
afternoon. HRRR/RAP soundings at Crosby show a deep isothermal 
layer that hovers near freezing until early Monday morning 
before cooling and remaining below freezing. But there is still 
support from other guidance for the deep isothermal layer to 
stay closer to freezing until late Monday afternoon, at which 
time precipitation may already be winding down there. NBM 
probabilities for measurable snowfall have increased, and are 
now as high as 40 to 60 percent across parts of Divide and Burke
Counties, and 20 to 40 percent in northern Williams County. The
probability for exceeding an inch of snow is no higher than 15 
percent in northwest Divide County, but the HREF maximum 
snowfall there is greater than 2 inches. However, these snow 
amounts and threshold probabilities are not fully taking into 
account lower snow-to-liquid ratios (less than 10:1) and the 
high probability of melting on contact with the warmer ground 
(in the absence of enhanced snowfall rates). It should be noted 
that there are steep lapse rates through and above the dendritic
growth zone, but the strongest forcing remains below the DGZ. 
The HREF probability for hourly snow rates exceeding just half 
an inch are less than 20 percent, rendering the 06Z HRRR's 
production of several inches of snow in Divide County a 
significant statistical outlier. 

Monday looks to be the coldest daytime period through at least 
Thursday, and possibly well beyond. Forecast highs range from 
the lower 40s northwest to mid 50s in the southern James River 
Valley. Would not be surprised to see maximum temperatures 
verify slightly cooler on Monday given the extensive cloud 
cover and precipitation, especially in the far northwest where, 
as mentioned above, there is a low probability of snow falling 
throughout the day. Despite precipitation moving out Monday 
night and surface high pressure beginning to build in, models 
show high confidence in an overcast sky persisting through the 
night. The probability of a widespread freeze Monday night 
continues to decrease, and we are now forecasting lows to remain
near to above freezing at most locations. 

On Tuesday, the western cutoff low is forecast to park over 
Utah. Flow aloft over the Northern Plains remains cyclonic with 
the passage of a northern stream shortwave, but underlying 
surface high pressure keeps precipitation chances around 10 
percent or less. Cloud cover could linger through the day 
though, and forecast highs only improve to around 50 to 55. The 
rest of the week continues to be marked by uncertainty in the 
evolution of the western cutoff low, as well as that of a potent
shortwave moving from British Columbia to the Great Lakes.
